Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Mara Ellis, who manages the grounds, learned about it when a camper came to the office shortly after breakfast. The camper’s small travel trailer had lights, but its refrigerator had switched to propane, and the outlet beside the picnic table showed no power. Mara thanked him for reporting the problem and asked him to leave the connection untouched until she could inspect it. The campground was nearly full, so she wanted to understand the fault before deciding whether the site could remain occupied.

Mara took the site map, a flashlight, and the campground’s voltage tester from the maintenance shed. Her colleague, Joel, met her at the equipment cabinet near the entrance to the row. They first checked the breaker labeled 18. It was not tripped, and the indicator on the cabinet did not show a fault. Joel suggested resetting the breaker, but Mara paused. The previous week, a loose cover had allowed rain into a different outlet, and she did not want to restore power before looking for signs of moisture or damage. They agreed to inspect the whole connection first.

At site 18, the pedestal stood on a gravel pad behind a low wooden border. Its metal door was closed, but the latch was stiff, and a narrow line of rust marked the lower edge. Mara used the flashlight to examine the housing before opening it. She saw no standing water, scorch marks, or exposed wire. The camper’s plug was disconnected and resting on a dry mat. Joel checked the exterior outlet with the tester while Mara watched the reading; the display stayed blank. They did not remove any covers or handle the internal wiring.

1. Inspection notes
   - The breaker for site 18 remained on and did not appear to be tripped.
   - The exterior outlet produced no reading on the campground’s tester.
   - The pedestal door had a stiff latch and a small rust line along its lower edge.
   - There was no visible standing water, scorching, or exposed wire.
   - The camper’s plug was disconnected and kept off the gravel.

Mara called the campground’s electrical contractor, Northline Service, and described what they had observed. The dispatcher asked whether the pedestal had been opened or reset. Mara said it had not been reset, and that they had only examined the exterior and tested the outlet. The dispatcher said a technician could visit that afternoon, but could not promise a precise arrival time until the morning schedule was complete. Mara wrote down the call time and the name of the dispatcher, then asked whether the contractor wanted the breaker left on. The dispatcher advised her to leave it as it was until a technician could inspect the connection.

Back at the office, Mara explained the situation to the camper. “We haven’t found a visible hazard, but the outlet isn’t supplying power, and we’re waiting for the contractor to inspect it,” she said. “Please keep your plug disconnected for now. I can move you to another powered site if you’d prefer, though the replacement site is farther from the washroom.” The camper asked whether the refrigerator could stay on propane overnight. Mara said that was a question for the camper’s appliance manual, not something she could confirm for him. He chose to remain at site 18 until the contractor arrived and said he would use propane in the meantime.

Mara checked the booking board before offering any move. Site 7 was vacant, but its power connection had been reserved for a late arrival, and the reservation notes requested a level pad close to the washroom. Site 22 was also powered and available, although it sat beside the service road. She called the incoming guest for site 7, who confirmed that the original location was still suitable. Mara did not move that reservation. She told the camper at site 18 that site 22 remained an option and made a note to keep it available until the electrical inspection was complete.

Joel placed a temporary notice on the pedestal stating that the connection was out of service and should not be used. He fixed the notice to the exterior handle without covering the campground’s site number or the contractor’s access point. Mara updated the maintenance log with the time of the report, the test result, and the contractor’s expected visit. She also recorded that the breaker had been left in its original position, following the dispatcher’s advice. At the daily staff check-in, she asked the evening host to keep guests away from the pedestal and to send any new reports directly to her rather than attempting a reset.

The technician had not arrived by midafternoon, so Mara called Northline Service again. The dispatcher confirmed that the visit was still on the schedule but said the technician was finishing a job elsewhere. Mara passed that information to the camper without giving a new arrival estimate. The camper had not changed his mind about moving, and the refrigerator was still operating on propane. Before the evening shift began, Mara checked that the notice remained attached, added the second call to the log, and told the evening host that no repair had yet been reported. The site’s power connection was still awaiting inspection when she handed over the office keys.

The campground’s office copy of the site map showed the location of the main shutoff, the equipment cabinet, and the numbered pedestals along each row. Mara returned it to the wall beside the maintenance log, where the evening host could find it. She left the contractor’s phone number on the work order and placed the site 18 key in its usual drawer.
